content: 1. Churcher TS, Ferguson NM, and Basáñez MG explored the concepts of density dependence and overdispersion in the transmission dynamics of helminth parasites, providing insights into their population biology and epidemiology. (Parasitology, 2005, 131(1):121-132) 2. Huppatz C and colleagues conducted a case study across five countries to derive lessons from the Pacific program aimed at eliminating lymphatic filariasis, emphasizing the challenges and successes of such large-scale public health initiatives. (BMC Infectious Diseases, 2009, 9:92) 3. Knopp S et al. analyzed the shifting patterns of soil-transmitted helminthiases in Zanzibar within the framework of national helminth control programs, highlighting the impact of interventions on disease prevalence and transmission. (American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, 2009, 81(6):1071-1078) 4. Bottomley C, Isham V, and Basáñez MG investigated the population biology of multi-species helminth infections, focusing on interspecific interactions and their influence on parasite distribution. (Parasitology, 2005, 131(3):417-433) 5. Fenton A examined the population dynamic consequences of co-infections involving microparasites and macroparasites, shedding light on their complex interactions and implications for disease control. (Parasitology, 2008, 135(13):1545-1560) 6. Fenton A, Lamb T, and Graham AL conducted an optimality analysis of Th1/Th2 immune responses during co-infections with microparasites and macroparasites, incorporating epidemiological feedback mechanisms. (Parasitology, 2008, 135(7):841-853) 7. Lello J et al. explored pathogen interactions, population cycles, and phase shifts, providing a deeper understanding of the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of infectious diseases. (American Naturalist, 2008, 171(2):176-182) 8. Gurarie D and King CH developed a heterogeneous model of schistosomiasis transmission, incorporating spatial variation and age-dependent factors to optimize drug therapy allocation for long-term control. (Parasitology, 2005, 130(1):49-65) 9. Gurarie D and Seto EY demonstrated how hydrologic and social connectivity sustain disease transmission in low-endemicity environments, using schistosomiasis as a model. (Journal of the Royal Society Interface, 2009, 6(35):495-508) 10. Waghorn TS et al. tested the hypothesis that leaving susceptible parasites in refugia could slow the development of anthelmintic resistance, providing evidence for or against this concept. (New Zealand Veterinary Journal, 2008, 56(4):158-163) 11. Anderson RM and May RM presented mathematical models to describe the population dynamics and control strategies for helminth infections in humans, offering a foundational framework for epidemiological studies. (Advances in Parasitology, 1985, 24:1-101) 12. Woolhouse ME discussed the application of mathematical models to understand the natural transmission dynamics of schistosome infections, emphasizing their utility in epidemiological research. (Acta Tropica, 1991, 49(4):241-270) 13. Duerr HP et al. examined the relationships between adult parasite burden, host age, and microfilarial density in human onchocerciasis, providing insights into the disease's epidemiology. (International Journal for Parasitology, 2004, 34(4):463-473) 14. Duerr HP et al. proposed that density-dependent parasite establishment in onchocerciasis may involve infection-associated immunosuppression as a key mechanism for regulating parasite density. (Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, 2003, 97(2):242-250) 15. Filipe JA et al. analyzed human infection patterns and heterogeneous exposure in river blindness, contributing to the understanding of disease transmission dynamics. (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, 2005, 102(42):15265-15270) 16. Plaisier AP et al. developed ONCHOSIM, a model and computer simulation program for studying the transmission and control of onchocerciasis, aiding in the design of intervention strategies. (Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine, 1990, 31(1):43-56) 17. Plaisier AP et al. estimated the required duration of combined annual ivermectin treatment and vector control in the Onchocerciasis Control Programme in West Africa, providing guidance for elimination efforts. (Bulletin of the World Health Organization, 1997, 75(3):237-245) 18. Winnen M et al. evaluated the potential of ivermectin mass treatments to eliminate onchocerciasis in Africa, discussing the feasibility and challenges of such interventions. (Bulletin of the World Health Organization, 2002, 80(5):384-391) 19. Woolhouse ME explored the application of mathematical models to control schistosome transmission dynamics, focusing on their role in designing effective intervention strategies. (Acta Tropica, 1992, 50(3):189-204) 20. Woolhouse ME examined the potential consequences of vaccination against human schistosomiasis, highlighting the implications for disease control and public health. (Vaccine, 1995, 13(12):1045-1050) 21. Chan MS, Woolhouse ME, and Bundy DAP assessed the long-term consequences of vaccination programs for human schistosomiasis, emphasizing the importance of sustained efforts. (Vaccine, 1997, 15(14):1545-1550) 22. Chan MS et al. developed EPIFIL, a dynamic model of infection and disease in lymphatic filariasis, providing a tool for understanding and controlling the disease. (American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, 1998, 59(4):606-614) 23. Norman RA et al. extended EPIFIL to include age-structured dynamics, enhancing its utility for describing the transmission and control of lymphatic filariasis. (Epidemiology and Infection, 2000, 124(3):529-541) 24. Michael E et al. discussed mathematical models for lymphatic filariasis control, focusing on endpoints and optimal intervention strategies. (Trends in Parasitology, 2006, 22(5):226-233) 25. Kyvsgaard NC, Johansen MV, and Carabin H simulated the transmission and control of Taenia solium infections using a Reed-Frost stochastic model, providing insights into disease dynamics. (International Journal for Parasitology, 2007, 37(5):547-558) 26. Torgerson PR reviewed mathematical models for controlling cystic echinococcosis, emphasizing their application in designing effective interventions. (Parasitology International, 2006, 55(Suppl):S253-258) 27. Roberts MG, Lawson JR, and Gemmell MA developed a mathematical model of the life cycles of Taenia hydatigena and T. ovis, contributing to the understanding of population dynamics in echinococcosis and cysticercosis. (Parasitology, 1987, 94(1):181-197) 28. Roberts MG discussed the modeling of parasitic populations, focusing on cestodes, and their implications for disease control. (Veterinary Parasitology, 1994, 54(1-3):145-160) 29. Brindley PJ et al. examined the implications of helminth genomics for human health, highlighting the potential for novel therapeutic and diagnostic approaches. (PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases, 2009, 3(10):e538) 30. Abubucker S et al. analyzed and classified the genome of the canine hookworm Ancylostoma caninum, providing insights into its biology and potential targets for intervention. (Molecular and Biochemical Parasitology, 2008, 157(2):187-192) 31. Zhou Y et al. revealed features of host-parasite interplay through the genome of Schistosoma japonicum, advancing the understanding of its biology and pathogenesis. (Nature, 2009, 460(7253):345-351) 32. Brindley PJ reviewed the molecular biology of schistosomes, emphasizing its relevance to understanding their pathogenicity and developing control strategies. (Trends in Parasitology, 2005, 21(11):533-536) 33. WHO's TDR Targets Database v4 serves as a chemogenomics resource for neglected tropical diseases, facilitating the prioritization of drug targets. (TDR, 2011) 34. Agüero F et al. prioritized drug targets on a genomic scale using the TDR Targets database, providing a framework for drug discovery in neglected tropical diseases. (Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, 2008, 7(11):900-907) 35. Spiliotis M et al. achieved transient transfection of Echinococcus multilocularis primary cells and complete in vitro regeneration of metacestode vesicles, advancing research on this parasite. (International Journal for Parasitology, 2008, 38(8-9):1025-1039) 36. Gobert GN et al. utilized transcriptomics to study the human Schistosoma blood flukes, identifying gene expression profiles associated with infection and host interaction. (Experimental Parasitology, 2006, 114(3):160-172) 37. Dillon GP et al. localized gene expression patterns in schistosomes using whole-mount in situ hybridization, providing insights into their developmental biology. (Parasitology, 2007, 134(11):1589-1597) 38. Hewitson JP, Grainger JR, and Maizels RM investigated the role of helminth-secreted proteins in modulating host immunity, highlighting their immunoregulatory functions. (Molecular and Biochemical Parasitology, 2009, 167(1):1-11) 39. Nacher M et al. found an association between intestinal helminth infections and increased incidence of Plasmodium falciparum malaria in Thailand, suggesting interactions between these infections. (Journal of Parasitology, 2002, 88(1):55-58) 40. Nacher M discussed the challenges of malaria vaccine trials in populations with high helminth prevalence, emphasizing the need to address co-infections. (Trends in Parasitology, 2001, 17(12):563-565) 41. Druilhe P, Tall A, and Sokhna C proposed that helminth infections could exacerbate malaria, advocating for integrated control strategies. (Trends in Parasitology, 2005, 21(8):359-362) 42. Murray MJ et al. linked parotid enlargement, forehead edema, and malaria suppression to the nutritional consequences of ascariasis, highlighting the complex interactions between nutrition and parasitic infections. (American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 1977, 30(12):2117-2121) 43. Murray J et al. explored the ecological and nutritional interrelationships between a host and two parasites, demonstrating the biological suppression of malaria. (American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 1978, 31(8):1363-1366) 44. Schijns VE reviewed immunological concepts of vaccine adjuvant activity, providing a basis for understanding their mechanisms of action. (Current Opinion in Immunology, 2000, 12(4):456-463) 45. Cooper PJ et al. observed impaired tetanus-specific immune responses in human onchocerciasis, potentially mediated by interleukin-10, and its implications for vaccine efficacy. (Journal of Infectious Diseases, 1998, 178(4):1133-1138) 46. Cooper PJ et al. associated Ascaris lumbricoides infection with a polarized cytokine response, contributing to the understanding of immune modulation by helminths. (Journal of Infectious Diseases, 2000, 182(4):1207-1213) 47. Sabin EA et al. reported impaired Th1-like immune responses to tetanus toxoid in individuals infected with Schistosoma mansoni, highlighting the impact of helminth infections on vaccine responses. (Journal of Infectious Diseases, 1996, 173(1):269-272) 48. Cooper PJ et al. found that Ascaris lumbricoides infection suppresses the interleukin-2 response to cholera toxin B subunit following vaccination with a live oral cholera vaccine. (Infection and Immunity, 2001, 69(3):1574-1580) 49. Hatherill M et al. discussed the potential impact of helminth infections on trials of novel tuberculosis vaccines, emphasizing the need to account for co-infections. (Vaccine, 2009, 27(35):4743-4744) 50. Cruz-Chan JV, Rosado-Vallado M, and Dumonteil E reviewed strategies to overcome the challenges posed by helminth infections in malaria vaccine efficacy trials. (Expert Review of Vaccines, 2010, 9(7):707-711) 51. Duke BOL and Moore PJ analyzed the contributions of different age groups to onchocerciasis transmission in a Cameroon forest village, providing insights into age-specific transmission dynamics. (Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, 1968, 62(1):22-28) 52. Abraham D, Lucius R, and Trees AJ reviewed immunity to Onchocerca spp. in animal hosts, contributing to the understanding of host-parasite interactions. (Trends in Parasitology, 2002, 18(4):164-171) 53. Njongmeta LM et al. found that cattle protected from onchocerciasis by ivermectin became highly susceptible to infection after drug withdrawal, highlighting the challenges of sustained control. (International Journal for Parasitology, 2004, 34(9):1069-1074) 54. Maizels RM et al. reviewed the regulation of pathogenesis and immunity in helminth infections, emphasizing the role of host-parasite interactions in disease outcomes. (Journal of Experimental Medicine, 2009, 206(10):2059-2066) 55. Shaw MA and Quinnell RJ discussed the role of human genetics in resistance to parasitic infections, providing insights into host susceptibility and immunity. (Parasite Immunology, 2009, 31(5):221-224) 56. Mas-Coma S, Valero MA, and Bargues MD provided a comprehensive overview of fascioliasis, including its transmission, epidemiology, and control strategies. (Advances in Parasitology, 2009, 69:41-146) 57. Rim HJ updated the knowledge on clonorchiasis, focusing on its epidemiology, pathogenesis, and control measures. (Journal of Helminthology, 2005, 79(3):269-281) 58. Sripa B reviewed the pathobiology of opisthorchiasis, providing an update on its clinical and molecular aspects. (Acta Tropica, 2003, 88(3):209-220) 59. Robinson MW et al. conducted an integrated transcriptomics and proteomics analysis of the secretome of Fasciola hepatica, identifying proteins associated with host invasion and infection. (Molecular & Cellular Proteomics, 2009, 8(8):1891-1907) 60. Kim YJ et al. demonstrated that excretory/secretory products from Clonorchis sinensis induce proliferative effects on human epithelial cells via regulation of the transcription factor E2F1. (Parasitology Research, 2008, 102(3):411-417) 61. Thuwajit C et al. showed that excretory/secretory products from Opisthorchis viverrini induce increased cell proliferation in mouse fibroblasts in vitro. (Parasitology, 2004, 129(4):455-464) 62. Bennuru S and Nutman TB reviewed lymphangiogenesis and lymphatic remodeling induced by filarial parasites, discussing their implications for pathogenesis. (PLoS Pathogens, 2009, 5(12):e1000688) 63. Freedman DO and Ottesen EA demonstrated that Schistosoma mansoni eggs stimulate endothelial cell proliferation in vitro, providing insights into the parasite's impact on host tissues. (Journal of Infectious Diseases, 1988, 158(3):556-562) 64. Bennuru S et al. profiled the excreted/secreted proteins of Brugia malayi at the host/parasite interface, identifying stageand gender-specific proteomic patterns. (PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases, 2009, 3(4):e410) 65. Higazi TB et al. investigated Wolbachia endosymbiont levels in severe and mild strains of Onchocerca volvulus, contributing to the understanding of strain-specific differences. (Molecular and Biochemical Parasitology, 2005, 141(1):109-112) 66. Griffin JT et al. used a model-based evaluation to assess strategies for reducing Plasmodium falciparum malaria transmission in Africa, providing evidence for effective interventions. (PLoS Medicine, 2010, 7(8):e1000324) 67. Shriram AN et al. studied the diurnal biting activity and transmission of Wuchereria bancrofti by Ochlerotatus niveus on the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, contributing to vector control efforts. (American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, 2005, 72(3):273-277) 68. Bockarie MJ et al. reviewed the role of vector control in the global program to eliminate lymphatic filariasis, emphasizing its importance in achieving elimination goals. (Annual Review of Entomology, 2009, 54:469-487) 69. Haas W et al. investigated the recognition of snail intermediate hosts by echinostome cercariae, providing insights into host-parasite interactions. (Parasitology, 1995, 110(2):133-142) 70. Kalbe M et al. studied the heritability of host-finding behavior in Schistosoma mansoni miracidia, contributing to the understanding of parasite adaptation. (Parasitology, 2004, 128(6):635-643) 71. Sukhdeo MVK and Sukhdeo SC reviewed trematode behaviors and their perceptual worlds, providing a unique perspective on parasite ecology. (Canadian Journal of Zoology, 2004, 82:292-315) 72. Gower CM and Webster JP discussed the fitness of indirectly transmitted pathogens, focusing on the constraints and trade-offs in their life cycles. (Evolution, 2004, 58(6):1178-1184) 73. Hassan AH et al. demonstrated that Schistosoma mansoni miracidia can differentiate between sympatric snail species, highlighting their host specificity. (Journal of Parasitology, 2003, 89(6):1248-1250) 74. Kalbe M, Haberl B, and Haas W studied the host-finding specificity of Schistosoma mansoni miracidia from an Egyptian strain, providing insights into their ecological adaptations. (Parasitology Research, 1996, 82(1):8-13) 75. Davies CM, Fairbrother E, and Webster JP examined mixed-strain schistosome infections in snails and their impact on the evolution of parasite virulence. (Parasitology, 2002, 124(1):31-38) 76. Norton A et al. investigated the simultaneous infection of Biomphalaria glabrata with Schistosoma mansoni and S. rodhaini, analyzing its effects on cercarial behavior and chronobiology. (Parasites & Vectors, 2008, 1(1):43) 77. Lu DB et al. studied the evolution of Schistosoma japonicum in multi-host systems, focusing on circadian rhythms and population genetics to understand host reservoir dynamics. (International Journal for Parasitology, 2009, 39(14):1581-1588) 78. Botros S et al. assessed the sensitivity of Schistosoma mansoni to praziquantel in a potential drug resistance focus in Egypt, providing critical data for treatment strategies. (International Journal for Parasitology, 2005, 35(7):787-791) 79. Pinlaor S et al. examined oxidative and nitrative stress in Opisthorchis viverrini-infected hamsters, highlighting the indirect effects of praziquantel treatment. (American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, 2008, 78(4):564-573) 80. Pinlaor S et al. demonstrated that repeated Opisthorchis viverrini infections induce the accumulation of DNA damage markers in the bile duct of hamsters, implicating nitric oxide synthase in carcinogenesis. (Carcinogenesis, 2004, 25(8):1535)
